Wording and speakers: Phineas and Ferb Wiki (Fandom) transcripts for The Fast and the Phineas and Lawn Gnome Beach Party of Terror

stories.title: Lawn Gnome Beach Party of Terror

notes: Every clip gets 0.5 s extra at the start and 1 s at the end (clipPadding), because caption times run ahead of the audio.
Some lines sit in the middle of a long caption chunk, so their start or end is an estimate. Clips may include one extra line.

Caption fixes (from Fandom): Isabella says "Whatcha doin'?" (captions: "What ya/What you doin'"). The radio DJ is Stanky Dog (captions: "Stinky Dog"). Buford says "Dinner-bell" (captions: "Jennabelle"). Candace talks to Stacy about Suzy (captions: "Sissy", "Susie"). Captions call Buford "Von Stomp". Fandom says "Van Stomm".
Running gags from S1 E1: "Whatcha doin'?", "Aren't you a little young…? Yes. Yes, I am." and Candace "in charge". New ones here: "so busted" and "Hey, where's Perry?"

Dropped because the YouTube captions don't include the line (covered by music or sound effects): Mom's stereo/"Mom, hurry up!" and the dandruff ad (5:22), Phineas "Ferb? Hello?" (7:02), Stacy's "I just saw Jeremy…" and Candace's "Jeremy's here? Gotta go!" (13:54). Also left out: most song lyrics, and "I've got 'em now" (6:48), where Fandom and the captions disagree.
One item comes from the end-credits song (mad skill, marked Sung). It is good for meaning but not ideal for pronunciation.

lines: That's better. What are you doing to Mom's car?!

expressions.meaning: "Trick out" = add lots of cool, fancy extras to something, like a car, bike or room.
expressions.listen: Candace's voice jumps up high on "Mom's car". She's shocked.
expressions.example: I tricked out my bike with lights and a horn.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher how you would make your bedroom super cool.

toneCards.situation: Show your friend the stickers and lights you put on your scooter.
Mom finds glitter all over her phone case. "I… tricked it out?"
toneCards.note: Same words, but now you're in trouble.

lines: You don't even know how to drive.
Well, duh. That's why Ferb built this remote.

expressions.meaning: "Duh" = "That's obvious!" You say it when someone tells you something everybody already knows.
expressions.tone: Friendly between kids. Said with an eye-roll, it's rude.
expressions.example: "It's raining." "Well, duh. Look at my wet hair!"
expressions.practice: Your friend says, "Ice cream is cold." Answer them.

toneCards.situation: Your friend says, "You like Lego, right?" while you're holding a giant Lego set.
Your teacher explains something and you say "Duh."
toneCards.note: To a grown-up this sounds rude. Say "Yes, I know" instead.

clips.label: At the race
lines: And your little brother's gonna be on TV!
Phineas? On TV? TV! That's it! They are so busted!

expressions.meaning: "Busted" = caught doing something wrong. "You're so busted" = you're in big trouble now. It's Candace's favorite line in every episode.
expressions.listen: In the garage, Candace says it in a deep, slow voice. That's how you know she's enjoying it.
expressions.example: Cookie crumbs on your face? You are so busted.
expressions.practice: You see your brother sneaking candy before dinner. What do you say?

toneCards.situation: You catch your brother playing video games after bedtime.
toneCards.note: Low and slow: "You are SO busted."

toneCards.situation: Your friend says they don't like cake, but they're on their third slice.
You hear Mom's car. The living room is a mess. "We are so busted!"

expressions.phrase: They won't get away with it!

lines: Heh, they won't get away with it this time!

expressions.meaning: "Get away with something" = do something wrong and not get caught or punished.
expressions.listen: "This time" is the joke. She has tried before and failed, and she'll fail again.
expressions.example: My brother ate my chocolate. He won't get away with it!
expressions.practice: Someone keeps taking the last cookie. Say they won't escape this time.

toneCards.situation: Someone keeps cutting in line at the slide.
Pretend you're a cartoon detective chasing a sock thief.
toneCards.note: Big, silly and over the top.

toneCards.situation: "He skipped his homework and the teacher didn't notice? How did he get away with that?"

lines: Oh, Candace, dear. Bubela, how good to see you. What a coincidence. Do you know your mom is here?
Yeah, I do, Mrs. Garcia-Shapiro. I need to talk to her if you don't mind.

expressions.meaning: A polite add-on that asks permission. But it can also mean "please let me get on with it."
expressions.tone: Polite words, but Candace says them fast and tight. She is in a hurry.
expressions.listen: Mrs. Garcia-Shapiro talks super fast. "Bubela" is a Yiddish word for "sweetie".
expressions.example: Can I sit here, if you don't mind?
expressions.practice: You want to get past someone blocking the door. Ask politely.

toneCards.situation: On a bus, you'd like to sit in the empty seat next to someone.
Your brother is standing in front of the TV during your show.

lines: Hi, boys! Well, if that's all, I'll just be getting back to the game.

expressions.plain: Well, if there's nothing else, I'll go back to my card game.
expressions.meaning: "If that's all" = if there's nothing else. A polite way to end a talk and go back to what you were doing.
expressions.tone: Mom isn't annoyed. She just doesn't see anything strange, because the car is already in the air.
expressions.example: If that's all, I'll go finish my homework.
expressions.practice: Your teacher finished checking your work. Politely say you'll go back to reading.

toneCards.situation: The doctor says you're all done. "If that's all, we'll head home."
Your sister interrupts your game for nothing important.
toneCards.note: Flat voice. You don't want to talk.

clips.label: Race car
lines: We're entering the Swamp Oil 500 today.

clips.label: Backyard beach
lines: Building a beach. Check it out.

expressions.plain: What are you doing? → Whatcha doin'?
expressions.meaning: "What are you doing?" said fast and sweet. Isabella says it in almost every episode. You met it in S1 E1.
expressions.listen: Both times she says "Hi, Phineas" in a dreamy voice first. That's part of the joke: she has a crush on him.
expressions.example: Hi, Grandpa! Whatcha doin'?
expressions.practice: Your teacher is drawing something. Ask about it the Isabella way.

toneCards.situation: You see your friend building a sandcastle.
Your brother is hiding something behind his back.

expressions.phrase: Aren't you gonna need…? / You're hired!

lines: Aren't you gonna need a pit crew?
Do you know a pit crew?
Well... I know a few people who work well together.
Great! You're hired! See you at the track.

expressions.meaning: "Aren't you gonna need…?" is a sneaky way to offer help. "You're hired!" = you've got the job. Kids say it as a joke when someone offers to help.
expressions.listen: "Gonna" = going to. Isabella says "I know a few people" like it's a secret. She means her own Fireside Girls troop.
expressions.example: "Aren't you gonna need someone to hold the ladder?" "Yes! You're hired!"
expressions.practice: Your teacher is carrying lots of books. Offer to help the sneaky way.

toneCards.situation: Your mom is baking. "Aren't you gonna need a taste-tester?"
Your friend offers to carry your bag. "You're hired!"
In a real interview, a boss says "You're hired" and means it.

expressions.meaning: Every episode, the boys notice their pet is gone. They never find out he's a secret agent. Fans love this line.
expressions.listen: Right after he asks, the music turns into spy music. That's your clue.
expressions.example: Hey, where's my other sock?
expressions.practice: Your pencil was just here a second ago. Ask about it the Phineas way.

toneCards.situation: Your cat was on the sofa a moment ago.
Your little brother was right behind you in the shop. Now he's not.
toneCards.note: Faster and higher. You really need an answer.

lines: Good morning, Agent P. The evil Dr. Doofenshmirtz is up to his old tricks.

expressions.meaning: Doing the same bad or naughty things again, like always.
expressions.example: The puppy is up to his old tricks. He chewed my shoe again!
expressions.practice: Your cat keeps knocking cups off the table. Tell your teacher about it.

toneCards.situation: Your little brother hid the TV remote again.
Grandpa tells the same silly joke every dinner.

lines: For reasons completely unknown, he's purchased a giant airship or blimp, as the kids say. Your mission is to find out why, and if necessary, put a stop to it.

expressions.meaning: Grown-ups say "as the kids say" before a cool new slang word. The joke: "blimp" isn't slang at all. It's a normal, old word.
expressions.listen: "Put a stop to it" = make it stop.
expressions.example: That movie was totally epic, as the kids say.
expressions.practice: Pretend you're a grandparent. Use a modern word with "as the kids say".

toneCards.situation: Pretend to be a grandparent: "That's very cool, as the kids say."
Your dad tries to use slang. "Nice, Dad. 'As the kids say.'"

expressions.phrase: Who, me? I'm a big fan of…

lines: Hey, Candace! I didn't know you were a racing fan!
Who, me? Oh, yeah! Yeah, I'm a big fan of those, those, uh... that red one is cute!
Oh, that's Billy Ray Digler's car. He's great.
clips.hl: I'm a big fan of those

expressions.meaning: "I'm a big fan of ___" = I really like ___. Candace is faking it. She knows nothing about racing, but she wants to impress her crush.
expressions.tone: The pauses and "uh" show she's making it up. "That red one is cute!" is not what a real racing fan would say.
expressions.listen: "Who, me?" = she's buying time to think.
expressions.example: I'm a big fan of chocolate chip cookies.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about a show or food you really love.

toneCards.situation: Tell a friend about your favorite band.
Someone asks if you like opera. You've never heard any. "Oh, yeah! I'm a big fan of… the, uh… singing?"
toneCards.note: The pauses and "uh" give you away.

lines: Now, is it just me, or does he look a little bit young to be behind the wheel of a 700-horsepower racing machine?

expressions.meaning: A polite way to say "I think…" and check if others agree. "Behind the wheel" = driving.
expressions.example: Is it just me, or is it really cold in here?
expressions.practice: You think the music is too loud. Check if your teacher agrees.

toneCards.situation: Is it just me, or does this milk smell funny?
Your brother takes his fifth cookie. "Is it just me, or are the cookies disappearing?"

expressions.phrase: A little young to…? Yes. Yes, I am.

clips.label: Racing announcers
lines: Now, is it just me, or does he look a little bit young to be behind the wheel of a 700-horsepower racing machine?

clips.label: Backyard beach
lines: Aren't you a little young to be a landscape contractor?

expressions.meaning: Someone says Phineas is too young. The answer agrees calmly, and then he does it anyway. This joke is from S1 E1, and it keeps coming back.
expressions.tone: Not rude. The double "Yes" makes it calm and confident.
expressions.listen: This time the announcer answers his own partner. Same joke, new speaker.
expressions.example: "Aren't you a little young to cook breakfast?" "Yes. Yes, I am."
expressions.practice: A grown-up asks if you're too young to build a big puzzle. Answer the Phineas way.

toneCards.situation: "Aren't you a little young to swim that far?"
"Aren't you a little young for that roller coaster?" "Yes, I am. I'll wait."
toneCards.note: Here you mean it and you stop.

lines: Hey, Candace is rooting for us!
Candace, you're on the big screen!

expressions.meaning: "Root for" = cheer for someone and hope they win. The joke: Candace is really yelling because she wants Phineas in trouble.
expressions.listen: "Root" rhymes with "boot".
expressions.example: I'm rooting for the blue team.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher which team or player you want to win.

toneCards.situation: Your best friend is in a race on sports day.
Your sister yells your name across the park because you're in trouble. You wave: "She's rooting for me!"

lines: All right. All right, Candace. This better be good.

expressions.plain: This better be good. = This had better be good. = It needs to be worth it.
expressions.meaning: "You interrupted me, so this had better be worth it." It's a gentle warning.
expressions.example: You woke me up? This better be good.
expressions.practice: Your brother calls you away from your favorite show. What do you say?

toneCards.situation: Your friend makes you stop your game to come and look at something.
Your friend says, "I've got a big surprise for you!" "Ooh, this better be good!"

expressions.phrase: Is there something you're trying to tell me?

lines: Candace, this is a dandruff commercial. Is there something you're trying to tell me?
clips.hl: Is there something you're trying to tell me?

expressions.meaning: "Are you hinting at something?" Mom jokes that Candace wants to say she has dandruff, which is flakes in your hair.
expressions.example: You gave me a toothbrush for my birthday. Is there something you're trying to tell me?
expressions.practice: Your friend gives you a book called "How to Be on Time". Answer them.

toneCards.situation: Your friend gives you soap as a present.
Your friend has been quiet all day.
toneCards.note: Kind voice: you really want them to talk.

lines: Ah, Perry the Platypus. I'm glad you're here. Actually, I was just getting ready to serve some platypus under glass! You're just in time to witness my latest invention…

expressions.meaning: "You arrived at the perfect moment." Usually friendly. From a villain, it's a threat.
expressions.listen: "Platypus under glass" is a joke on a fancy restaurant dish. He's pretending he'll cook Perry.
expressions.example: You're just in time for pizza!
expressions.practice: Your teacher arrives just as you finish a drawing. Welcome them.

toneCards.situation: Your friend walks in right as the pizza arrives.
Your friend walks into your blanket fort. "Ah, you're just in time to witness… my pillow cannon!"

lines: After which, I will deflate everything in the Tri-State Area! That way, if anyone wants anything flated, they will have to talk to me.

plain: Real words: deflate (air out), inflate (air in).
He means: "If anyone wants anything inflated, they'll need me."
But he says "flated", which isn't a word. He sounds clever, but he isn't.
expressions.meaning: "Deflate" = let the air out. "Inflate" = put air in. Doofenshmirtz chops off the front and makes up "flate". It isn't a real word. That's the joke.
expressions.example: If you want your balloon inflated, ask me. I have the pump!
expressions.practice: Make up a silly word by cutting the front off a real word (try "unhappy").

toneCards.situation: Announce to your family that you control all the bubbles in the bathtub.
Your friend says "flate". "You mean inflate!"

expressions.phrase: You are in big trouble, mister!

lines: Phineas, you are in big trouble, mister—!

expressions.meaning: "Mister" here isn't polite. Parents say "young man" or "mister" when they scold a boy. Candace copies a parent's voice.
expressions.example: You ate all the cookies? You are in big trouble, mister!
expressions.practice: Pretend to be a parent scolding a teddy bear.

toneCards.situation: Your dog dug up the garden. "You're in big trouble, mister!"
Your friend steals your fries as a joke.

lines: Smile! Souvenir picture? Only a dollar.

expressions.meaning: A kind way to tell someone they have something on their face. You stop and point instead of saying "You look dirty."
expressions.listen: Jeremy doesn't finish the sentence. You don't need to. The point says the rest.
expressions.example: You've got a little… ketchup, right there.
expressions.practice: Your teacher has chalk on their nose. Tell them kindly.

toneCards.situation: Your friend has ice cream on their chin. Point to your own chin.
A grown-up you don't know well has spinach in their teeth.
toneCards.note: Quiet voice and a small point.

lines: Hey hey, Missy. Two pictures, two bucks.
Oh, yeah, uh, I've only got a dollar, but uh, I just want the one. You can just tear the other one up, 'kay?

expressions.meaning: "Buck" = a dollar (American slang). "Missy" is what a grown-up calls a girl when telling her off.
expressions.listen: Candace says "the one" = the one picture she wants, the one with Phineas.
expressions.example: This comic costs five bucks.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher how much your favorite snack costs, using "bucks".

toneCards.situation: Tell a friend your new pen was only two bucks.
A grown-up stops a kid taking a free sample: "Hey, missy, that's one per person."
toneCards.note: "Missy" sounds bossy. Don't say it to grown-ups.

expressions.phrase: see what this puppy can do

lines: Hey, Ferb. Do you think we can get any more power? I mean, I know it's just a battery. But I was thinking: Let's open it up and see what this puppy can—

expressions.meaning: "This puppy" = this thing (a machine, car or gadget). "Open it up" = go full speed. "See what it can do" = test how good it is.
expressions.example: New bike! Let's see what this puppy can do.
expressions.practice: You got a new remote-control car. Tell your teacher you want to test it.

toneCards.situation: You get a brand-new skateboard.
Someone hears "this puppy" and looks for a dog.

expressions.phrase: Now that's what I'm talkin' about!

lines: Oh yeah! Now that's what I'm talkin' about!

expressions.meaning: "Yes! This is exactly what I wanted!" You shout it when something goes really well.
expressions.listen: "Talkin'" drops the g. Stress "THAT'S".
expressions.example: Pizza for dinner? Now that's what I'm talkin' about!
expressions.practice: Your teacher says there's no homework today. React.

toneCards.situation: Your team scores the winning goal.
Your brother finally cleans one sock off the floor. "Wow. That's what I'm talkin' about."
toneCards.note: Flat voice. You mean the opposite.

lines: Well, Mom, what do you think of this?

expressions.plain: You've looked better (before). = You don't look great right now.
expressions.meaning: A soft way to say "You don't look good right now." Candace wanted Mom to see Phineas. Mom only sees burnt, messy Candace.
expressions.example: "How's my hair after the wind?" "You've looked better."
expressions.practice: Your friend just got out of a muddy race. They ask how they look.

toneCards.situation: Your friend asks how they look after a long, sweaty game.
Your friend wakes up with crazy bed hair.
Your friend looks pale and sick. "You've looked better. Are you OK?"

lines: Hmm. I suppose I should've seen that coming.

expressions.meaning: "I should have guessed that would happen." You say it after something goes wrong that was easy to predict.
expressions.listen: "Should've" = should have, said "SHOULD-uv".
expressions.example: I left my ice cream in the sun. I should've seen that coming.
expressions.practice: You stacked your blocks really high and they fell. What do you say?

toneCards.situation: You tease the cat and it scratches you.
You trip over the shoe you left on the stairs.
Your brother forgets his lunch again. "I should've seen that coming!"

expressions.phrase: That's good, Candace. Go watch a little TV.

lines: Wait a minute. I bet it's still on TV!
That's good, Candace. Go watch a little TV.

expressions.meaning: Mom isn't really listening. She says something nice so Candace will leave her alone. "I bet…" = I'm pretty sure.
expressions.tone: Flat and bored. "That's good" here means "Sure, sure, whatever."
expressions.example: I bet it's still in my backpack!
expressions.practice: You're pretty sure your lost toy is under the bed. Say it with "I bet".

toneCards.situation: Your little brother tells you about his dream for the tenth time. "That's nice. Go play."
Your friend feels sick. "That's OK. Go watch a little TV and rest."

plain: Full version: "It looks like we'll have to walk home."
Drop "It" and use "we're walking" for the plan. You get "Looks like we're walking."
expressions.meaning: Their car was just stolen, but Phineas stays calm. He makes a plain, short comment instead of panicking. That's the joke.
expressions.example: The bus left without us. Looks like we're walking.
expressions.practice: Your pencil broke and there's no sharpener. Say it the calm Phineas way.

toneCards.situation: The elevator is broken. Looks like we're taking the stairs.
It's raining and Dad forgot the car keys.

lines: "Why don't you go back home, Candace?" "I'm busy with my bridge game, Candace." She has no idea!

expressions.meaning: "She doesn't understand at all." Candace also copies Mom in a silly voice. That's a mocking voice: you repeat someone to make fun of them.
expressions.tone: The mocking voice is OK in a cartoon. To a real person's face, it's rude.
expressions.example: My dad thinks this game is easy. He has no idea!
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about a grown-up who doesn't know how hard something is.

toneCards.situation: Nobody believes you saw a raccoon in the kitchen.
Your mom has no idea about the surprise party.

lines: It's beautiful! I gotta admit, I thought you were exaggerating a bit, but this is really worth getting excited about!

expressions.meaning: "I have to admit" = I'll be honest, I was wrong. "Worth getting excited about" = good enough to be excited.
expressions.tone: Mom praises the clean car, not the race car. Candace is stuck with her mouth open.
expressions.listen: "Gotta" = got to = have to.
expressions.example: I gotta admit, I thought broccoli was gross, but this is yummy.
expressions.practice: You didn't want to go to the museum, but it was fun. Tell your teacher.

toneCards.situation: You thought the new teacher would be strict, but they're fun.
Your brother's joke is actually funny. "OK, I gotta admit, that was good."
toneCards.note: You don't want to say it, but you do.

expressions.meaning: Candace's jaw has dropped in shock. A jaw-drop means you're super surprised. Mom gently reminds her she looks silly.
expressions.example: Close your mouth, you'll catch flies!
expressions.practice: Your friend is staring with their mouth open at a huge cake. Tease them gently.

toneCards.situation: Your little sister stares at the fireworks with her mouth open.
Someone keeps talking. "Close your mouth!"
toneCards.note: Without "Honey", it means "Be quiet!" That's rude.

expressions.phrase: take it easy / blow the day off

lines: Unless you live at the beach, I say take it easy and do nothin' today. Yup, just find yourself a shady tree, and maybe an aquatic mammal of some sort, and blow the whole day off.

expressions.meaning: "Take it easy" = relax. "Blow the day off" = skip all your plans and do nothing. "An aquatic mammal" is a joke: the boys are lying with Perry the platypus.
expressions.listen: "Nothin'" drops the g. "Yup" = yes.
expressions.example: It's Sunday. Let's take it easy.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher how you'd spend a lazy Sunday.

toneCards.situation: It's a holiday and you have no plans.
Your friend is shouting about a lost game. "Hey, take it easy."

expressions.phrase: If we let ___ stop us, then ___ wins.

lines: Come on, Ferb. If we let a little heat stop us from having the best day ever, then the morning DJs win.

expressions.meaning: A funny way to say "Don't give up!" You pretend the problem is an enemy that wins if you quit.
expressions.example: If we let a little rain stop our picnic, then the clouds win!
expressions.practice: It's cold outside, but you want to go to the park. Convince your teacher.

toneCards.situation: Your team is losing at halftime.
You're too sleepy for breakfast. "If I let sleepiness stop me, the pancakes win!"

lines: So what are you up to?
We're making our own beach, right here in the backyard.
Oh, how cute. Well, I'm off for my spa day.

expressions.meaning: Mom thinks it's a little sandbox game. "How cute" can mean "That's sweet, but not serious." "I'm off" = I'm leaving now.
expressions.tone: Mom says it kindly, but she doesn't believe them. Later, the beach is huge.
expressions.example: Oh, how cute! A baby duck!
expressions.practice: Your little cousin says they'll build a real rocket. React like a grown-up who doesn't believe it.

toneCards.situation: You see a puppy in a tiny raincoat.
Your big brother laughs at your plan: "Oh, how cute."
toneCards.note: It can feel mean. It means "You're just a little kid."

lines: You heard her. We can't bug Dad, which makes me in charge… by default.

expressions.meaning: "By default" = because nobody else can. Candace is the boss only because Dad's busy. "Bug" = bother. "Carry on" = keep going (a bossy way to end a talk).
expressions.listen: Candace pauses before "by default". It's like she knows it isn't a great reason. (In S1 E1, she was "in charge" too!)
expressions.example: Nobody else wanted to be goalie, so I'm goalie by default.
expressions.practice: You won a game because the other player went home. Explain it to your teacher.

toneCards.situation: Mom goes out. "I'm the oldest, so I'm in charge… by default. Carry on."
You won the race because you were the only runner. "I won by default."

lines: We suspect Doofenshmirtz. Get right on it.

expressions.meaning: "Start doing this right now!" A boss gives an order. Or someone promises: "I'll get right on it."
expressions.example: "Can you clean your room?" "I'll get right on it!"
expressions.practice: Your teacher asks you to read a page. Promise to start now.

toneCards.situation: Mom asks you to set the table.
"Clean your room!" "Sure… I'll get right on it," you say, still lying on the sofa.

lines: I don't care if they're lab partners! We're locker neighbors. And locker neighbors trumps lab partners any day.

expressions.meaning: "Trumps" = beats, is more important than. "Any day" = always, no question. Candace is arguing about which friend matters more.
expressions.listen: "Gotta go" = I have to go. Very common way to end a phone call fast.
expressions.example: Pizza trumps salad any day.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher which is better: summer or winter. Use "any day".

toneCards.situation: You and a friend argue about which superhero is best.
"Ice cream or broccoli?" "Ice cream trumps broccoli any day!"

lines: Hah! You call that a beach? This is WAY below your usual standard. This isn't even worth a call to Mom.

expressions.meaning: "That's not a real ___!" It's a teasing put-down. Candace thinks it's just a sandbox, so it isn't even worth telling Mom.
expressions.listen: "WAY below" is stressed. Way = very much.
expressions.example: You call that a sandcastle? Watch this!
expressions.practice: Your friend draws a tiny dog. Tease them, then say something nice.

toneCards.situation: Your friend shows you a tiny snowman.
Someone shows you their drawing. "You call that art?"
toneCards.note: This hurts feelings. Don't say it about real effort.

toneCards.situation: You hold up your burnt toast. "You call this breakfast?"

expressions.phrase: If you ever want to ___, you're gonna have to ___.

lines: You know, if you guys ever want to be popular, you're gonna have to stop playing in sandboxes.

expressions.meaning: Bossy big-sister advice: "If you want X, you must do Y."
expressions.listen: Then a beach ball hits her. Know-it-alls get what's coming in cartoons.
expressions.example: If you ever want to be a chef, you're gonna have to try new foods.
expressions.practice: Give your teacher some advice about learning to skateboard.

toneCards.situation: Tell your little brother how to be cool.
Your friend wants to swim faster. "You're gonna have to practice every day."

lines: Oh no, wait, wait, wait. That was the garage door opener. You are mine now! And that was the TV remote. I've got to start labeling these things.
clips.hl: I've got to start labeling these things

expressions.meaning: "I need to begin doing this from now on." You say it after a mistake shows you need a new habit.
expressions.tone: "You are mine now!" is supposed to be scary, but he keeps pressing the wrong button. It gets funnier each time.
expressions.example: I lost my keys again. I've got to start using a key hook.
expressions.practice: You keep forgetting your water bottle at school. Say what you'll do from now on.

toneCards.situation: You put salt in your tea instead of sugar.
You wear two different shoes to school.

expressions.phrase: I can see our house from up here!

lines: Hey, look! I can see our house from up here!
clips.hl: I can see our house from up here!

expressions.meaning: A classic joke line people say when they're very high up. Here it's funny because the house is right next to the beach.
expressions.example: We're on the top of the Ferris wheel. I can see our house from up here!
expressions.practice: You're on the top bunk bed. Make the joke.

toneCards.situation: You're at the top of a tall tower.
You stand on a chair. "Whoa! I can see our house from up here!"
toneCards.note: It's funny because it isn't high at all.

lines: I've never been happier in my entire life!
Something is very wrong. Not a single call from Candace. Not even a text message.

expressions.meaning: The joke: Mom is worried because things are quiet. Candace calls all the time, so no calls means something is up. "Not a single ___, not even a ___" = nothing at all.
expressions.listen: Right before, Candace says "I've never been happier in my entire life!" Happy and worried, back to back.
expressions.example: Not a single sound from the kids. Not even a giggle. Something is very wrong.
expressions.practice: Your noisy dog is totally quiet. Tell your teacher why you're worried.

toneCards.situation: Your little brother has been quiet in his room for an hour.
You smell smoke in the kitchen.

expressions.phrase: My only companion was the moon… and my neighbor Kenny.

lines: My only companion was the moon. And my neighbor Kenny.

expressions.meaning: A sad, dramatic sentence, then a normal, silly ending. This is called an anticlimax. "Companion" = friend who keeps you company.
expressions.example: My only friend at camp was a frog… and my cousin Ben.
expressions.practice: Tell a sad, dramatic story about waiting at the doctor's, then add a silly ending.

toneCards.situation: Tell your family about a "terrible" day with no dessert.
Pause a long time before the silly part.

lines: Hello, Buford. Perhaps you missed the sign.

expressions.meaning: Polite words with a sharp meaning: "There's a rule. Follow it." "Out of my way" = move (rude).
expressions.tone: "Perhaps" sounds polite, but Phineas is standing up to a bully.
expressions.listen: "Dinner-bell" is Buford's mean nickname for a girl in Isabella's troop.
expressions.example: Perhaps you missed the sign. No dogs allowed.
expressions.practice: Someone is running by the pool. Remind them of the rule, politely but firmly.

toneCards.situation: Someone cuts in line at the water fountain.
"Out of my way!" to someone in the hallway.

expressions.phrase: I don't like this any more than you do.

lines: I don't like this any more than you do.

expressions.meaning: "I don't like it either. We're both stuck with it." The joke: the sign stops yodeling too, so the yodeler is sad.
expressions.listen: He speaks with a funny mountain accent, because yodeling is a kind of mountain singing.
expressions.example: I don't like the rain any more than you do, but we need to walk.
expressions.practice: Your friend complains about a long car ride. Say you feel the same.

toneCards.situation: You and your brother both have to do chores.
Your little sister complains about bedtime. "I don't like it any more than you do, but rules are rules."

lines: First up in the surf contest is Bobby Nelson. Oh! And Nelson eats it on the five-footer!

expressions.meaning: "Eat it" = fall or crash badly, especially on a board or bike. "A five-footer" = a wave five feet tall.
expressions.example: I tried a skateboard trick and totally ate it.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about a time you fell off something.

toneCards.situation: Your friend slips on the ice, but they're fine.
Someone gets hurt falling. Don't laugh. Ask: "Are you OK?"

lines: Uh-oh, what's this? Oh, those kids today and their holographic projections.

expressions.meaning: What grumpy old people say about young people's new stuff. The joke: Phineas used a hologram (a 3-D light picture) to dodge the bully.
expressions.example: Those kids today and their video games!
expressions.practice: Pretend to be a grumpy grandparent talking about phones.

toneCards.situation: Complain about kids and their scooters.
Your dad can't work the TV. You say, "Those kids today and their remotes!"

lines: He's in the pipeline, now he's hangin' ten! He's hanging twenty! He's hangin' thirty-two! Now he's just hangin'! The crowd loves it!

expressions.meaning: "Hang ten" = a surf move with all ten toes over the board's edge. The numbers get silly. Then "just hangin'" also means "just chilling, relaxing".
expressions.example: "What are you doing?" "Nothing, just hangin'."
expressions.practice: Your teacher asks what you did on Saturday. Say you relaxed, the slang way.

toneCards.situation: A friend texts "What's up?" You answer "Just hangin'."
Pretend to be a surf announcer.

lines: It seems Phineas Flynn's radical surfing has made judge #3 re-think Einstein's theory of relativity! Cowabunga, laws of nature!

expressions.meaning: "Cowabunga!" = an old surfer shout of joy. "Radical" = awesome (old surf slang). The joke: his surfing breaks the rules of science.
expressions.example: Cowabunga! Let's jump in the pool!
expressions.practice: You're about to jump into a big pile of leaves. Shout it.

toneCards.situation: You jump into the swimming pool.
Dad says "Cowabunga!" and you groan.

lines: I'm right around the corner; I'll be there in two minutes.

expressions.meaning: "Very close by." It can also mean "coming very soon": "Summer is right around the corner."
expressions.listen: "Wait, what?!" jumps up high. That's shock.
expressions.example: Wait for me. I'm right around the corner!
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher that your birthday is coming soon.

toneCards.situation: Call your friend: you're almost at their house.
"The holidays are right around the corner!"
Mom is right around the corner and your room is a mess.

expressions.phrase: Run for your lives! It's gnome-ageddon!

lines: Run for your lives!! It's gnome-ageddon!!!

expressions.meaning: "Run for your lives!" = a silly panic shout. "Armageddon" = the end of the world. Add "gnome" and you get a gnome disaster.
expressions.example: Run for your lives! It's the tickle monster!
expressions.practice: Your little brother is chasing everyone with a water gun. Shout a warning.

toneCards.situation: Your dad is coming with a tickle attack.
Your room is full of Lego. "It's Lego-geddon!"

expressions.phrase: Tell me the truth. What is going on here?

lines: Candace, tell me the truth. What is going on here?

expressions.meaning: A parent's serious question. It means "Don't make up a story."
expressions.example: Tell me the truth. Did you eat my cookie?
expressions.practice: Your toy is broken and your brother looks guilty. Ask him.

toneCards.situation: Find paint all over the bathroom.
Your friend looks sad but says "I'm fine."

expressions.phrase: just like they said… it turned out to be…

lines: Phineas and Ferb built a beach in the backyard, just like they said they were going to. But instead of just a cute little beach in their sandbox; it turned out to be this absolutely huge beach, with a coastline, and palm trees, and a pier…
clips.hl: just like they said they were going to

plain: "just like they said they were going to" is missing the end.
Full: "just like they said they were going to (build one)."
English often drops the end when it's obvious.
expressions.meaning: "Turn out to be" = end up being (often a surprise). Candace talks super fast, listing everything in one breath.
expressions.example: The test turned out to be easy.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about something that turned out better than you expected.

toneCards.situation: The scary movie turned out to be funny.
Tell your whole day in one breath: "And then, and then, and then…"

lines: …and just for a moment, it seemed that the wily Buford would steal away the coveted surfing trophy from under the noses of our heroes…

expressions.meaning: "Under someone's nose" = right in front of them, but they don't notice. "Wily" = sneaky. "Coveted" = that everyone wants.
expressions.listen: Candace is now talking like a TV sports announcer. The water is draining away behind her.
expressions.example: The cat stole the fish right from under our noses!
expressions.practice: Your brother took the last cookie while you were looking. Tell your teacher.

toneCards.situation: Tell your friend about the soccer game like a sports announcer.
Someone took your seat right under your nose.

expressions.phrase: Just let me have my moment!

lines: …then I can only continue my benign reign and spread love, happiness and ultimate popularity throughout my kingdom! If you would just let me have my moment!

expressions.meaning: "Let me enjoy this special time, please!" You say it when someone interrupts your happy moment. "Benign reign" = kind rule, like a nice queen.
expressions.example: I finally won! Let me have my moment!
expressions.practice: You scored a goal and your friend is already talking about something else.

toneCards.situation: Your brother interrupts your birthday wish.
You did one push-up and pose like a champion.

lines: Candace, honey, I think it's time to get you out of the sun for a little while.

expressions.meaning: Phineas says it calmly while Candace is being led away, upset. It's an understatement, a big feeling said in small words. "Get you out of the sun" = Mom thinks Candace is acting strange from the heat.
expressions.example: My brother cried and laughed at the movie. I think he liked it.
expressions.practice: Your friend screamed all the way down the water slide. Comment on it.

toneCards.situation: Your little sister fell asleep in her cake at the party. "I think she had fun."
Your grandma danced all night at the wedding.

lines: And speaking of hot, slather on the sunscreen listeners, 'cause tomorrow's weather calls for another scorcher.
With a slight chance of scattered lawn gnomes.

expressions.meaning: "A scorcher" = a very hot day. "Calls for" = says will happen. Ferb finishes in weather-report words, but it's raining gnomes.
expressions.listen: "Speaking of ___" = changing the topic using a word just said.
expressions.example: Wear a hat. Today's going to be a scorcher.
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher what the weather will be like tomorrow, weather-report style.

toneCards.situation: Give tomorrow's weather like you're on the radio.
"Tomorrow: sunny, with a slight chance of… homework."

lines: He's got more than just mad skill, he's got a beaver tail and a bill!

expressions.meaning: "Mad skills" = amazing skills. "Mad" here means very, not angry. Usually people say "mad skills".
expressions.tone: Sung, so use it for meaning, not pronunciation.
expressions.example: Did you see her dribble the ball? She's got mad skills!
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about someone who's amazing at something.

toneCards.situation: Your friend solves a puzzle cube super fast.
You flip a pancake. "Mad skills!"
